chapter_summary:
Managing user and group accounts is a fundamental aspect of system administration, and automating these tasks with Ansible brings significant efficiency and consistency, especially across a large number of servers. Instead of manually logging into each machine to run `useradd`, `usermod`, `userdel`, `groupadd`, or `groupdel` commands, Ansible allows you to define the desired state of your users and groups in a declarative playbook. This ensures that all systems conform to a standardized access policy, reducing human error and improving security posture.

The core of user management in Ansible lies with the `ansible.builtin.user` module. This module is incredibly versatile and allows you to perform a wide range of operations. To create a new user, you typically specify the `name` and `state: present`. For instance, to create a user named `devops_user`, you would use `name: devops_user state: present`. Beyond simple creation, you can define the user's `uid` (User ID), `home` directory, `shell`, `password` (though using `password` directly in playbooks is generally discouraged due to security, and `authorized_key` for SSH access is preferred), and even `comment` for descriptive purposes. When setting a password, it's critical to use a hashed password generated by `mkpasswd -m sha-512` or `python -c 'import crypt; print(crypt.crypt("your_password", crypt.mksalt(crypt.METHOD_SHA512)))'` rather than plain text. Ansible will then ensure that the user exists with these specified attributes. If the user already exists but with different attributes, Ansible will modify them to match the playbook's definition.

```yaml
- name: Create a new system user
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: appuser
    comment: "Application Service User"
    uid: 1001
    home: /opt/appuser
    shell: /sbin/nologin
    state: present
    password: "$6$saltsalt$hashedpasswordhere" # Use a securely generated hash
```

Similarly, the `ansible.builtin.group` module handles group management. You can create a new group with `name` and `state: present`, and specify its `gid` (Group ID). For example, `name: developers state: present gid: 2000`. Once groups are created, you can assign users to them. The `ansible.builtin.user` module includes a `groups` parameter, which accepts a comma-separated list of secondary groups. A common mistake here is to simply list the groups without also specifying `append: yes`. If `append: yes` is omitted, Ansible will remove the user from any groups not explicitly listed in the `groups` parameter, potentially revoking legitimate access. Always remember to use `append: yes` when you intend to add a user to additional groups without affecting their existing secondary group memberships.

```yaml
- name: Ensure 'developers' group exists
  ansible.builtin.group:
    name: developers
    gid: 2000
    state: present

- name: Add 'devops_user' to 'developers' group
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: devops_user
    groups: developers
    append: yes
    state: present # Ensure user also exists
```

When it comes to deleting users or groups, the `state: absent` parameter is used. For users, `state: absent` will remove the user account. You can also specify `remove: yes` to delete the user's home directory and mail spool, which is often desired for complete cleanup. For groups, `state: absent` will remove the group, but it's important to ensure no users are primarily associated with that group before deletion, as this can lead to orphaned files. Always consider the implications of deletion and ensure proper backups or data migration if necessary. A common safety note is to always test user/group management playbooks on non-production or staging environments first, especially when deleting accounts, to prevent accidental data loss or access issues. Additionally, ensure your automation adheres to your organization's identity and access management (IAM) policies and auditing requirements.

screens.title: Automating User and Group Management
screens.subtitle: Declarative users and groups with Ansible for consistent system access

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on automating user and group management using Ansible so you stop performing manual account changes on each server. You will learn the practical behavior of the ansible. builtin. user and ansible. builtin. group modules, how UID and GID are used, and why append is critical when adding secondary groups. We'll also cover safe deletion practices and verification commands you can run after automation. As a concrete example, you'll see how to create a qa_team group and two users qa_lead and qa_engineer with fixed UIDs and shells, and how to verify their presence with id and getent group. This matters because declarative playbooks make access consistent, reduce human error, and let you meet auditing policies across many hosts. A common pitfall — accidentally removing a user's existing secondary groups — will be highlighted and corrected with append: yes. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to author idempotent tasks for users and groups, test them safely in staging, and reason about when to remove home directories or preserve data during deletions. Consider what account policies your organization requires and how automation will enforce them consistently.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use Ansible's user and group modules to declare desired account state across systems; prefer hashed passwords, authorized_key for SSH, and append: yes when adding secondary groups.

narration.text: These objectives map to practical tasks you'll perform with Ansible. First, you'll learn how to create, modify, and delete local user accounts using the ansible. builtin. user module, including setting attributes like UID, home, and shell. Second, you'll manage local groups via ansible. builtin. group and assign users to primary and secondary groups so you can control resource access consistently. Third, you'll identify attributes such as UID and GID and how they relate to file ownership and access, plus why using hashed passwords or authorized_key is preferred. Fourth, you'll learn common pitfalls: notably the append behavior which, when omitted, will replace a user's secondary groups and can inadvertently revoke access. Each objective includes a milestone so you can confirm competency by running a playbook to create a group and users and verify them with id and getent group on a staging host. These skills matter because they reduce manual errors, make audits simpler, and let you scale identity changes across many systems with repeatable results.

keyIdea.text: Practice declarative user/group tasks, verify UID/GID behavior, use secure credential handling, and avoid append-related pitfalls.

screens.subtitle: Run, test, and verify playbooks without risking production

narration.text: This second objectives slide emphasizes safe execution and verification. You'll practice writing playbooks that are idempotent so running them multiple times leaves systems in the same desired state. We'll set up a staging host and run the manage_qa_users. yml example to create a qa_team group and two users. After a playbook run you'll use commands like id qa_lead and getent group qa_team to confirm group membership and UIDs. For deletion tasks we'll highlight remove: yes to clean home directories, and explain why that must be tested before applying in production. We'll also discuss secure handling of credentials: prefer hashed passwords generated by system tools or use authorized_key to deploy SSH keys rather than storing plain text passwords. Finally, you'll learn a short verification checklist: test in staging, confirm id and getent output, and audit file ownership for migrated data. These steps reduce risk and help maintain compliance with access policies.

narration.text: The ansible. builtin. user module is the primary tool you use to declare local user accounts on managed hosts. At its simplest, you set name and state: present to ensure an account exists. But production-ready playbooks specify attributes: uid to fix a numeric user ID, home for a predictable location, shell to control login behavior, and comment to describe the account. For authentication, avoid plain text passwords in playbooks; instead use hashed passwords generated with system tools or manage SSH access with authorized_key entries. A concrete example is creating an app user with uid 1001, home set to /opt/appuser, and shell set to /sbin/nologin so the account cannot log in interactively. A common misconception is that specifying password in plain text is safe if the playbook is private; it is not. Use secrets management or hashed values. Another pitfall is assuming state: present will not change existing attributes — Ansible will modify attributes to match your declaration when they differ. Key takeaway: express the exact desired state and manage secrets securely. How will you ensure hashed passwords or SSH keys are used in your environment?

keyIdea.title: User module summary
keyIdea.text: Declare users with attributes like uid, home, shell; prefer hashed passwords and authorized_key for SSH rather than plain text.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › ansible.builtin.user deep dive
What the user module does
Ensure an account exists with exact attributes and manage group membership.
Key attributes
  • name and state: present/absent
  • uid, home, shell, comment
  • password (use hashed) and authorized_key for SSH access
Common misconceptions
Some expect plain-text passwords are acceptable or that present won't change existing attributes — both are unsafe assumptions.
Key Takeaway

Always declare exact attributes for predictable accounts and avoid plain-text credentials in playbooks.

Concrete example
- name: Create a new system user
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: appuser
    comment: "Application Service User"
    uid: 1001
    home: /opt/appuser
    shell: /sbin/nologin
    state: present
    password: "$6$saltsalt$hashedpasswordhere"
Example explanation
  • UID fixes numeric identity across hosts.
  • Non-login shell prevents interactive sessions for a service account.
  • Hashed password used to avoid exposing secrets in playbook text.
Misuse to avoid
Storing plain text passwords in playbooks or assuming that present will never change an existing account's attributes.

narration.text: The ansible. builtin. group module declaratively manages system groups. Use name and state: present to create a group and gid when you need a fixed numeric group identifier. Fixing GIDs matters when several hosts must share file ownership mappings or when migrating data so that file permissions remain consistent. A concrete example from our chapter is creating a developers group with gid 2000. The module also supports state: absent to remove a group, but you must check whether any user still has that group as their primary group to avoid orphaned ownership. A common misconception is that deleting a group is harmless; in reality, removing a primary group for users can cause files to be left without an expected group owner. Always verify no critical files depend on the group, or reassign ownership before deletion. Key takeaway: declare groups with explicit gid when deterministic ownership is required and validate consequences before removing groups. ansible.builtin.group module means use the group module to create groups with specific gids when you need deterministic ownership; validate primary group usage before removal.. In practical terms, creating groups and understanding gid. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Group module summary
keyIdea.text: Use the group module to create groups with specific GIDs when you need deterministic ownership; validate primary group usage before removal.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Group management
Group creation and GID
Use gid for consistent numeric identities across systems.
Example
- name: Ensure 'developers' group exists
  ansible.builtin.group:
    name: developers
    gid: 2000
    state: present
Why GID matters
  • File ownership uses numeric GID; fixed GIDs keep permissions stable across hosts.
  • Migrating data between systems benefits from matching numeric IDs.
Safe removal
Before setting state: absent, ensure no user has the group as their primary group and reassign any critical file ownership.
Misconception
Deleting a group is not risk-free; it may leave files with unexpected ownership or cause access issues.
Key Takeaway

Declare GIDs when you need deterministic ownership and audit primary group usage before deletion.

screens.title: Primary vs Secondary Groups
screens.subtitle: How primary and supplementary memberships affect access

narration.text: Understanding the difference between primary and secondary (supplementary) groups is essential when assigning users. A user's primary group is the one listed in their account entry and is typically used as the default group owner for newly created files. Secondary groups are additional memberships that grant access to other group-owned resources. When adding a user to a secondary group via the ansible. builtin. user module, the groups parameter sets the full list of supplementary groups; omitting append: yes will replace existing secondary groups with the list you specify. For example, if john currently belongs to groups alpha and beta and you run a task that sets groups: project_alpha without append: yes, john will lose alpha and beta and only be in project_alpha. A correct form uses append: yes to preserve existing memberships while adding new ones. A common misconception is that groups acts like an additive toggle — in truth it replaces the supplementary group list unless append is set. The takeaway: when your intent is to add membership, always use append: yes to avoid accidentally revoking access. Primary vs Secondary Groups means groups replaces supplementary groups by default; use append: yes to add memberships without removing existing ones.. In practical terms, how primary and supplementary memberships affect access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Group assignment rule
keyIdea.text: groups replaces supplementary groups by default; use append: yes to add memberships without removing existing ones.

content.html:

Primary Group
The user's main group; often matches the username and sets default file group owner.
Example
User qa_lead with primary group qa_team results in new files owned by gid 2005 by default.
Secondary Groups
Additional groups granting access to group-owned resources; managed with the groups parameter.
Pitfall
Using groups without append: yes will replace all supplementary groups, possibly removing legitimate access.
Correct pattern to add membership
- name: Add 'devops_user' to 'developers' group
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: devops_user
    groups: developers
    append: yes
    state: present

screens.title: Hands-on: manage_qa_users.yml walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Idempotent playbook to create qa_team and two users

narration.text: Let's walk through the manage_qa_users. yml example that creates a qa_team group and two users. The playbook begins with hosts and become: true since user and group tasks require elevated privileges. First task ensures the group exists using ansible. builtin. group with name qa_team, gid 2005, and state: present. Next tasks create qa_lead and qa_engineer users with specified UIDs, /bin/bash shells, and groups: qa_team. Note the append: yes parameter — this ensures that if these users already have other supplementary groups, those memberships are preserved while adding qa_team. Idempotency is achieved because the modules declare the desired state; running the playbook again will not create duplicates or change accounts unnecessarily. A concrete run example: execute ansible-playbook -i inventory. ini manage_qa_users. yml and then verify using id and getent. A common mistake is forgetting become: true; without privileges the tasks will fail. After you run it once on staging, re-run to confirm idempotency and review the module output for changed: 0 on subsequent runs. How will you structure inventories to target only staging hosts first? Hands-on: manage_qa_users.yml walkthrough means use become: true, ensure group first, create users with uid and shell, and set append: yes to preserve existing memberships.. In practical terms, idempotent playbook to create qa_team and two users. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Playbook pattern
keyIdea.text: Use become: true, ensure group first, create users with uid and shell, and set append: yes to preserve existing memberships.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › manage_qa_users.yml walkthrough
Playbook template
---
- name: Manage QA team users and groups
  hosts: all
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure 'qa_team' group exists
      ansible.builtin.group:
        name: qa_team
        gid: 2005
        state: present

    - name: Create 'qa_lead' user and add to 'qa_team'
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: qa_lead
        uid: 1005
        shell: /bin/bash
        groups: qa_team
        append: yes
        state: present

    - name: Create 'qa_engineer' user and add to 'qa_team'
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: qa_engineer
        uid: 1006
        shell: /bin/bash
        groups: qa_team
        append: yes
        state: present
Execution notes
  • become: true is required for system changes.
  • Creating group first avoids race conditions when assigning groups to users.
  • append: yes prevents accidental loss of other supplementary groups.
Terminal demo snippet
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini manage_qa_users.yml
PLAY RECAP *****************************************************************
target1                : ok=4    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0

# Verify
$ id qa_lead
uid=1005(qa_lead) gid=2005(qa_team) groups=2005(qa_team)
Checklist
Run in staging, confirm changed: values, re-run to verify idempotency, then push to production when safe.

screens.title: Deleting users and safe cleanup
screens.subtitle: state: absent, remove: yes, and migration concerns

narration.text: Deleting an account requires care. The user module supports state: absent to remove an account and remove: yes to delete the user's home directory and mail spool. This is useful for cleaning up after offboarding, but it can lead to data loss if home directories contain important artifacts. A recommended process is: first archive or migrate any needed files, then run a controlled playbook with state: absent and remove: yes on staging to verify behavior. A concrete example task removes old_employee entirely by setting state: absent and remove: yes. A frequent misconception is that remove: yes will also remove files owned by the user that live outside the home directory; it will not automatically fix ownership of those files. You should check for files owned by the UID across the filesystem before deletion and reassign ownership if necessary. Key takeaway: deletion is irreversible from the system's perspective; always back up, validate file ownership, and test in non-production before removal. Deleting users and safe cleanup means use remove: yes for complete cleanup only after backing up and confirming no critical files are left elsewhere with that uid.. In practical terms, state: absent, remove: yes, and migration concerns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe deletion
keyIdea.text: Use remove: yes for complete cleanup only after backing up and confirming no critical files are left elsewhere with that UID.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Delete & cleanup
Removal pattern
Archive, reassign ownership, then remove user account with remove: yes.
Example: complete removal
- name: Remove old_employee completely
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: old_employee
    state: absent
    remove: yes
Checklist before deletion
  • Backup or archive home directory.
  • Find files owned by the user's UID outside home and reassign.
  • Test removal in staging to confirm expected cleanup.
Misconception
remove: yes does not hunt for all files owned by the user across the filesystem; it deletes home and mail spool only.
Practical tip
Use find with -uid to locate orphaned files and reassign ownership before deletion.
Key Takeaway

Deletion requires backup and ownership checks; test in staging before production removal.

screens.title: Password handling and SSH keys
screens.subtitle: Use hashed passwords or authorized_key for authentication

narration.text: Authentication for automated user creation requires special handling. The user module supports a password field, but you should never place plain-text passwords in playbooks. The recommended practice is to use hashed passwords generated by system utilities such as mkpasswd with sha-512 or appropriate crypt tools, and place the hash into the password parameter. Even better, for service and administrative access, prefer authorized_key entries to deploy SSH public keys for users. A concrete example in the chapter shows using a hashed password string in the password parameter for appuser. A common misconception is that Ansible will automatically hash plain-text passwords for you; it will not. Another misconception is that authorized_key is only for interactive users — it is appropriate for any account that needs SSH access. When you manage keys, use vault or secrets management to protect private keys and hashes. The takeaway: avoid plain text, use hashed values or SSH keys, and secure secrets with vault or your secrets backend. Password handling and SSH keys means never store plain-text passwords. use hashed passwords or authorized_key and protect secrets with ansible vault or a secrets backend.. In practical terms, use hashed passwords or authorized_key for authentication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Secure credentials
keyIdea.text: Never store plain-text passwords. Use hashed passwords or authorized_key and protect secrets with Ansible Vault or a secrets backend.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Password & SSH key practices
Hashed passwords
Generate a hashed password locally and store the hash in the playbook or secrets store.
password: "$6$saltsalt$hashedpasswordhere"
Why hashes?
  • Prevents exposing credentials if playbooks are stored in version control.
  • Hashes are required by many systems for direct assignment to /etc/shadow.
authorized_key
Deploy public SSH keys to grant secure, passwordless access.
Practical example
Use the authorized_key parameter to add a public key string to a user's authorized_keys file and protect it with vault when necessary.
Misconception
Ansible will not hash plain-text passwords for you; pre-hash or use keys and protect secrets externally.

screens.title: Idempotency and expected playbook output
screens.subtitle: Interpreting changed vs ok and re-running safely

narration.text: Idempotency is the guarantee that running the same playbook multiple times yields the same final state and does not repeatedly perform changes. The user and group modules are designed to be idempotent: when attributes already match the declared state Ansible reports ok rather than changed. On the first run you expect changed: 1 or more for new accounts; subsequent runs should report changed: 0 or changed: 0 for those tasks. A concrete experiment is to run the manage_qa_users. yml playbook twice against a staging host. The first run will create the group and users; the second should report that those tasks are ok and changed: 0. A common misconception is that idempotency equals immutability; it doesn't — if you change the playbook to adjust an attribute, the module will update the resource to match the new declaration. When analyzing output, pay attention to failed tasks and to whether become: true was applied. Key takeaway: use repeated runs in staging to validate idempotency and inspect changed counts to confirm the playbook has stabilized. Idempotency and expected playbook output means run playbooks multiple times to verify changed counts drop to zero; changes are applied only when declared state differs from the host state.. In practical terms, interpreting changed vs ok and re-running safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Idempotency rule
keyIdea.text: Run playbooks multiple times to verify changed counts drop to zero; changes are applied only when declared state differs from the host state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Idempotency
Expected run behavior
First run creates resources; subsequent runs should be no-op when nothing changed.
PLAY RECAP *****************************************************************
target1                : ok=4    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0
# Second run:
target1                : ok=4    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0
Testing approach
  • Run in staging, observe changed counts.
  • Modify playbook to change an attribute and confirm Ansible updates the host.
  • Use ansible-playbook's check mode for dry-run insight, but note some modules cannot fully predict changes.
Key Takeaway

Idempotency makes automation safe to rerun; use repeated runs to confirm stability and changed counts to spot intended updates.

screens.title: Verification commands and quick checks
screens.subtitle: Using id and getent to confirm account state

narration.text: After applying changes with Ansible, simple system commands confirm results. Use id username to show a user's uid, primary group, and supplementary groups. Use getent group groupname to inspect group membership and verify the GID. In our QA scenario, id qa_lead should reveal uid 1005 and gid 2005, while getent group qa_team lists the members. These commands are fast and available on most Unix-like systems, making them ideal for quick verification in staging. A practical tip is to script post-playbook checks into your CI pipeline so verification is automated. A common misconception is that absence of error output equals success; always confirm account attributes explicitly. Also, when users are deleted, id returns a non-zero status; check the output carefully. Key takeaway: integrate id and getent checks into your verification steps to confirm UIDs, GIDs, and memberships after automation. Verification commands and quick checks means use id and getent group to validate uid, gid, and group membership after playbook runs; automate these checks where possible.. In practical terms, using id and getent to confirm account state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use id and getent group to validate UID, GID, and group membership after playbook runs; automate these checks where possible.

uid=1005(qa_lead) gid=2005(qa_team) groups=2005(qa_team)

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: append, privileges, and testing strategies

narration.text: This lesson highlights recurring mistakes and how to avoid them. The first is forgetting append: yes when adding a user to supplementary groups; without it you replace the user's entire supplementary group list and may remove essential access. Second, failing to use become: true causes playbook tasks that manage system accounts to fail due to insufficient privileges. Third, storing plain-text passwords in playbooks exposes credentials; use hashed passwords or authorized_key and protect secrets with Ansible Vault. Fourth, running destructive tasks like state: absent without backups can lead to irreversible data loss. To avoid these, follow a testing strategy: create a staging inventory, run playbooks there, inspect changed counts, and use id/getent to validate. Another useful practice is to implement small, targeted tasks rather than broad changes so you can reason about each change easily. The takeaway: combine careful parameter choices with disciplined testing to prevent common automation disasters. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means always use append: yes to add groups, run tasks with become, protect credentials, and test deletions in staging first.. In practical terms, append, privileges, and testing strategies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid automation hazards

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Lab: QA team
Starter playbook
---
- name: Manage QA team users and groups
  hosts: all
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure 'qa_team' group exists
      ansible.builtin.group:
        name: qa_team
        gid: 2005
        state: present

    - name: Create 'qa_lead' user and add to 'qa_team'
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: qa_lead
        uid: 1005
        shell: /bin/bash
        groups: qa_team
        append: yes
        state: present

    - name: Create 'qa_engineer' user and add to 'qa_team'
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: qa_engineer
        uid: 1006
        shell: /bin/bash
        groups: qa_team
        append: yes
        state: present
Verification steps
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini manage_qa_users.yml
$ id qa_lead
$ id qa_engineer
$ getent group qa_team
Remember

Run first in staging, review changed counts, then promote the playbook to production once verified.

narration.text: These are the concise concepts to remember as you automate user and group management. The ansible. builtin. user module creates, modifies, and removes user accounts and handles attributes like uid, home, shell, and password. The ansible. builtin. group module manages groups and gid and should be used before assigning users to that group. UID and GID are numeric identifiers that determine file ownership and access. The state parameter ensures presence or absence of resources, and append: yes prevents accidental removal of supplementary group memberships. Use hashed passwords or authorized_key for authentication and protect secrets with vault or a secrets backend. Always test playbooks in staging, verify results with id and getent group, and back up data before using remove: yes. Keep these items in mind when authoring playbooks so your automation is safe, repeatable, and auditable.
